primary_sources: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek Treaty), September 17, 1851

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek Treaty), September 17, 1851, Articles 1, 2, 3, and 7, as signed. Public domain. Note: the Senate ratified the treaty with an amendment changing the Article 7 annuity from fifty years to ten years (plus up to five discretionary years), May 24, 1852.
stimulus.text: The aforesaid nations... do hereby covenant and agree to abstain in future from all hostilities whatever against each other... The aforesaid nations do hereby recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts, within their respective territories... In consideration of the rights and privileges acknowledged in the preceding article, the United States bind themselves to protect the aforesaid Indian nations against the commission of all depredations by the people of the said United States... the United States bind themselves to deliver to the said Indian nations the sum of Fifty thousand dollars per annum for fifty years in provisions, merchandize, domestic animals and agricultural implement.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Treaty of Fort Laramie, September 17, 1851, public domain
stem: According to the treaty, the United States promised the Indian nations which of the following?

options.text: Protection against wrongs committed by American citizens.
Citizenship in the United States for all tribal members.
options.misconception: The treaty promises protection and annuities, not citizenship.

options.text: Ownership of all land west of the Mississippi River.
options.misconception: The treaty defined tribal territories; it did not grant all land west of the Mississippi.

options.text: The right to remove American settlers from Oregon.
options.misconception: The treaty gave the United States the right to build roads and posts in tribal territory, not the reverse.

rationales.A: The treaty says the United States binds itself “to protect the aforesaid Indian nations against the commission of all depredations by the people of the said United States.”
rationales.B: Citizenship is not mentioned in the treaty; the promises are protection and yearly goods.
rationales.C: The treaty defined each nation's territory; it did not hand over all land west of the Mississippi.
rationales.D: The treaty recognized the United States' right to build roads and military posts in tribal territory, the opposite of removal.
rationales.general:
1. Find the American promise. The United States binds itself “to protect the aforesaid Indian nations against... depredations by the people of the said United States.”
2. Read it plainly. The government promised to stop its own citizens from harming the tribes.
3. Check the rest. No citizenship, no continent-wide grant, and no removal of settlers is promised.
Remember: a treaty has two sides. Here the tribes promised peace and the United States promised protection — read both promises before judging the deal.
